items.title: Analysis argues AI industry spending and growth may justify valuations despite concerns of a bubble [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
items.summary:
The article challenges the common belief that the AI industry is in a speculative bubble poised to burst, suggesting that the rapid growth and high valuations of AI companies could be justified. It highlights that while AI companies have committed trillions in spending, much of this is one-time infrastructure investment, and ongoing operational costs are comparatively lower, with some companies already showing profitability beyond compute expenses.

Supporting details include estimates of AI industry spending reaching around $5 trillion, with debt repayments potentially manageable given the revenue scale of major tech firms. The article cites Anthropic's S-1 filing showing rapid revenue growth and profitability metrics, indicating that AI companies may sustain and grow profits as adoption expands. It also notes that AI's potential applications remain underutilized, suggesting further growth opportunities beyond current levels.

items.title: Goldman Sachs restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and GitHub Copilot to engineers, barring traders and bankers from AI coding tools amid risk and productivity concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Goldman Sachs is pulling Claude Code from its bankers and traders
items.summary:
Goldman Sachs has limited access to Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub Copilot to its engineering staff, cutting off traders and bankers who previously used these AI tools to monitor client flows and build market models. This change follows an internal review addressing productivity and risk, with the updated guidance implemented in October and earlier restrictions applied in Hong Kong.

While engineers and quantitative researchers retain access, most non-engineering staff are now barred from using AI coding agents that can write and execute code independently. Goldman continues to collaborate closely with Anthropic, serving as a lead underwriter on its upcoming IPO, and maintains internal AI assistants managed by engineering teams. The restrictions aim to mitigate risks related to code oversight, information barriers, and compliance on trading desks.

items.title: Developer organizes AI-assisted coding tasks into a git-based priority queue to reduce cognitive overload and improve focus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
items.summary:
A developer describes a method to manage multiple AI-generated coding tasks by organizing them as markdown tickets in a git repository, creating a priority queue that preserves context and state outside of chat windows or memory. An agent processes these tickets in cycles, handling research, builds, tests, and deployment checks, while decisions requiring human judgment are funneled into a prioritized inbox for review.

This system allows the developer to focus on one task at a time, closing each ticket after action to prevent mental overload and distraction. The approach addresses challenges of sequencing and context management in AI-assisted workflows, improving productivity despite ongoing tooling refinements and the inherent exhaustion of the work.

items.title: Developer switches from Anthropic's Claude Code to Pi citing stability and usability issues despite recent feature updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Goodbye Claude, hello Pi
items.summary:
A longtime user of Anthropic's Claude Code has decided to stop using it as their main coding tool and switch to Pi due to accumulated frustrations with Claude Code's usability and frequent disruptive updates. The user appreciated Claude Code's early capabilities but found its integration with VSCode limited, its GUI extension buggy, and its rapid feature additions lacking focus and stability.

The user noted that Anthropic's recent attempt to retain them by adding AGENTS.md file support came too late. They criticized the frequent system prompt changes and excessive overhead in Claude Code compared to Pi, which offers a more stable and minimalist experience. The post reflects on the challenges of pioneering AI coding tools and expresses hope for Pi's clearer vision and smoother operation.

items.title: Researchers formalize do-calculus completeness and show it is incomplete for universal identifiability in causal effect estimation
items.originalTitle: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability
items.summary:
Researchers study the problem of identifying causal effects from arbitrary observational and interventional data, termed Universal Identifiability (uID), which generalizes classical identifiability problems. They propose a formal definition of do-calculus completeness and confirm previous completeness results for classical cases but demonstrate that do-calculus rules are incomplete for the more general uID problem.

The work explains why the uID problem has remained unresolved, as existing do-calculus methods cannot fully address it. This highlights limitations in current causal inference tools when dealing with complex identification scenarios involving diverse data sources.
items.description:
Researchers study the problem of identifying causal effects from arbitrary observational and interventional data, termed Universal Identifiability (uID), which generalizes classical identifiability problems. They propose a formal definition of do-calculus completeness and confirm previous completeness results for classical cases but demonstrate that do-calculus rules are incomplete for the more general uID problem.

The work explains why the uID problem has remained unresolved, as existing do-calculus methods cannot fully address it. This highlights limitations in current causal inference tools when dealing with complex identification scenarios involving diverse data sources.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of causal effect identification from an arbitrary set of observational and/or interventional distributions, which we call Universal Identifiability (uID). The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both sound and complete in these problems. Despite these well-established results, a formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However, for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus far.

items.title: Researchers propose Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection method to improve reasoning distillation in smaller language models, achieving state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection for Reasoning Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), a method designed to enhance training of smaller language models by focusing on the student's failure modes and selecting teacher-generated reasoning trajectories that the student can realistically reproduce. This approach addresses the common issue of students overfitting teacher outputs and failing to generalize when their inference behavior deviates from training data.

FPRT profiles student errors through repeated sampling to identify distinct failure types, then uses tailored prompting strategies to generate candidate solutions from the teacher. It selects the candidate whose initial corrective reasoning steps after divergence are most reproducible by the student, targeting the primary bottleneck in reasoning correction. Experiments demonstrate that FPRT outperforms existing methods across five benchmarks and multiple student model architectures.

Researchers introduce Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), a method designed to enhance training of smaller language models by focusing on the student's failure modes and selecting teacher-generated reasoning trajectories that the student can realistically reproduce. This approach addresses the common issue of students overfitting teacher outputs and failing to generalize when their inference behavior deviates from training data.

FPRT profiles student errors through repeated sampling to identify distinct failure types, then uses tailored prompting strategies to generate candidate solutions from the teacher. It selects the candidate whose initial corrective reasoning steps after divergence are most reproducible by the student, targeting the primary bottleneck in reasoning correction. Experiments demonstrate that FPRT outperforms existing methods across five benchmarks and multiple student model architectures.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training smaller language models on reasoning solutions generated by a larger teacher model is the prevailing approach for transferring mathematical reasoning capabilities. However, the student tends to overfit the output distribution of the teacher and generalizes poorly when its own behavior at inference time deviates from the training data. Recent methods attempt to bridge this gap by incorporating error data, yet the corrective trajectories still reflect the reasoning patterns of the teacher, which the student cannot reliably reproduce, leaving the distribution mismatch largely unresolved. We propose a method, Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), built on the insight that effective training data should be jointly determined by what the student fails on and what it can realistically learn. Our method first profiles the failure behavior of the student on each problem through repeated sampling, characterizing it in terms of error rate and error consistency to reveal qualitatively distinct failure modes. Each mode demands a fundamentally different training signal. The diagnosed mode then guides candidate generation from the teacher via distinct prompting strategies tailored to each failure type. Among the correct candidates, our method selects the one whose initial reasoning steps after the point of divergence are most reproducible by the student. These first corrective steps constitute the primary bottleneck, while the remaining steps follow an already corrected context and can therefore be continued more readily. This contrasts with standard reranking approaches, which score the trajectory as a whole and thereby dilute the signal at the critical reasoning transition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves the SOTA performance across the five benchmarks on both student backbones.

items.title: Researchers propose Query-Guided Positional Modulation to mitigate lost-in-the-middle issue in long-context language models by reshaping rotary position embeddings using query relevance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers identify that long-context language models often lose information in the middle of inputs due to decay in rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which weakens positional signals between distant tokens. To address this, they propose Query-Guided Positional Modulation (QGPM), a training-free method that adjusts RoPE positions based on query relevance derived from the model's own attention heads, improving information retrieval within long contexts.

QGPM creates broad relevance maps in lower layers and sharper ones in upper layers, advancing low-relevance tokens slightly on fast-rotating planes to pull relevant evidence closer to queries while preserving original token layout on slow-rotating planes. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER benchmarks across multiple context lengths show that QGPM outperforms base models and strong baselines, especially in retrieval tasks, and generalizes across different model backbones. The researchers have made their code publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.

items.title: Researchers introduce LambdaMix, a parameter-efficient method using jointly trained low-rank adapters for multi-objective preference optimization in language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
items.summary:
Researchers present LambdaMix, a new method that enables language models to adapt to changing user preferences by jointly training low-rank adapters for multiple objectives over a frozen base model. This approach allows a single training run to support varying preference vectors at inference without further optimization, improving flexibility in balancing competing goals such as helpfulness and harmlessness.

The team tested LambdaMix on four models across tasks including instruction-following math problems and comment rewriting to reduce personal attribute clues. LambdaMix outperformed existing conditioned and policy merging baselines in terms of hypervolume, used fewer training completions, and required less storage than specialist policies. The method achieves wider score ranges and higher coverage by varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together, demonstrating efficient multi-objective optimization in language model deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

items.title: Researchers find subliminal learning transfers hidden preferences in vision-language models through unrelated training tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers studied subliminal learning in vision-language models (VLMs) by finetuning teacher models to prefer specific animals or facial attributes and then training student models on unrelated visual tasks using outputs from these teachers. They found that students trained on biased teacher outputs showed a preference for the target attributes, with differences up to about 10 percentage points, indicating that hidden preferences can transfer through unrelated training data. This effect was observed across VLMs ranging from 2 billion to 7 billion parameters and varied with training data size, target preference, model, and output generation method.

The study also showed that biased students used more similar language in their explanations to the biased teachers than control students did, even when selecting the same images. These findings highlight that training VLMs on unrelated data can influence both their image preferences and explanatory behavior, with transfer effects strengthening as more training samples are used.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.

items.title: Researchers develop dual-stream LLM-guided reward design for reject-inference-aware reinforcement learning to improve e-commerce payment fraud detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dual-Stream LLM-Guided Reward Design for Reject-Inference-Aware Reinforcement Learning in E-Commerce Payment Fraud Detection
items.summary:
Researchers propose a dual-stream reward design guided by a large language model (LLM) to address the reject-inference problem in e-commerce payment fraud detection, where legacy blocked transactions lack fraud labels, causing biased training data. The LLM designs a reward combining labeled transaction precision and scoring of legacy-blocked unlabeled transactions by contrasting new risk signals with legacy scores, allowing the model to select relevant evidence based on evaluation feedback and producing auditable reward code.

In tests over a four-month out-of-time period, the dual-stream agent outperforms prior labeled-only agents and production baselines in dollar-weighted precision at multiple recall levels without adding inference cost, maintaining the same policy architecture as previous work. This approach improves fraud detection accuracy by incorporating information from previously unlabeled blocked transactions through reinforcement learning guided by LLM-designed rewards.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Production fraud-detection models learn from a censored slice of their own traffic: transactions a legacy system blocked never receive fraud labels, so models train on a biased, approved-only distribution. We extend LLM-guided reward design, the framework of Qu et al. (2025) in which an LLM evolves the reward of a two-step REINFORCE fraud-blocking policy, to attack this reject-inference problem inside the reward. A single LLM designs a dual-stream reward: stream 1 applies the standard dollar-weighted precision objective to labeled transactions; stream 2 scores legacy-blocked, unlabeled transactions by contrasting the newest gradient-boosted risk signal against the legacy scores that drove the original block. Rather than prescribe which signals matter, we expose a superset of evidence and let the LLM decide for itself which to use, guided by evaluation feedback alone; because it writes the reward as code, that choice is directly auditable. On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the dual-stream agent beats the prior labeled-only agent at every target recall, by +4.7, +2.4 and +3.0 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80%, 85% and 90% recall, and the production baseline by +6.8 points on average. The resulting policy is architecturally identical to that of Qu et al. (2025) and adds no inference cost.

items.title: Researchers propose reversible LLM-based rule overlay to patch blind spots in frozen gradient-boosted fraud detectors, improving recall and precision without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Patching the Blind Spots: Reversible LLM Rule Overlay for Frozen Fraud Detectors
items.summary:
Researchers propose a framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate rules addressing underweighted features in frozen gradient-boosted fraud detection models, creating a reversible log-lift overlay that enhances performance without modifying the original model. This approach pools outputs from three diverse LLM backbones to reduce variance and applies the overlay at production cut-offs, improving recall by 2.26% at equal precision and precision by 1.60% at equal recall on a real-world e-commerce fraud detector.

The method was tested on a public benchmark with seven bias-shift variants, consistently improving precision at equal recall while maintaining neutral recall at equal precision. Each rule amendment is interpretable, naming the specific fraud pattern it covers, offering a practical way to patch deployed fraud detectors without the risks associated with retraining.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In industrial tabular fraud classification, gradient-boosted trees remain state-of-the-art, but even a well-trained model has blind spots, and retraining the deployed model is not always safe. We propose a framework that patches such a model without modifying it: LLMs propose rules anchored on features the model underweights by SHAP, and the resulting noisy pool is screened for empirical support and calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay that runs at the production cut-off. Single-LLM benefit is high-variance and inverts between datasets, so we pool three diverse backbones by equal-weight logit averaging, trading peak gain for a bounded worst case. On a real-world e-commerce fraud detector trained on selection-biased data, continued training regresses even when carefully tuned, whereas the overlay gains on average +2.26% recall at equal precision ($\Delta$R@P) and +1.60% precision at equal recall ($\Delta$P@R) over production cut-offs spanning 30-57% precision and 23-63% recall. On a public benchmark of seven designed bias-shift variants it raises $\Delta$P@R on every variant and keeps $\Delta$R@P near neutral. Each amendment is a readable predicate naming the fraud pattern it covers.

items.title: Researchers propose Jacobian-causal memory control for persistent memory in language models, introducing a method to select and verify memory interventions with theoretical performance bounds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
items.summary: Researchers introduce Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), a system for managing persistent memory in language models by predicting and verifying the influence of memory interventions to control their effects and side effects. The approach includes theoretical guarantees under certain assumptions and compares JCMC with existing retrieval baselines using a new evaluation protocol without reporting benchmark results. The study highlights conditions under which simpler methods might match JCMC's performance, suggesting areas for further validation and comparison.

The approach includes theoretical guarantees under certain assumptions and compares JCMC with existing retrieval baselines using a new evaluation protocol without reporting benchmark results. The study highlights conditions under which simpler methods might match JCMC's performance, suggesting areas for further validation and comparison.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

items.title: Researchers introduce RPEG, a graph-based system optimizing training pipelines for reasoning language models, improving performance and hardware utilization on up to 256 GH200 GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
items.summary:
Researchers present the RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG), a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation designed to optimize the structure and execution of reinforcement learning pipelines for reasoning language models. items.title: Researchers develop methods to recover skill documents from LoRA adapters, restoring up to 91% of original task performance on external skills [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
items.summary: Researchers investigated whether skill documents, which teach language models specific tasks and are often compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), can be recovered from these adapters and their frozen base models. They found that directly reading adapter weights yielded minimal recovery, but using a trained Executing Writer on the adapted model recovered 39-44% of key instructions and restored 85-91% of task gains on 41 external skills. For adapters trained only on behavior, recovery was more challenging, but an agent comparing base and adapted models could recover 58-71% of LoRA gains and transfer skills to models unable to load the original adapter, significantly improving performance on benchmarks like ALFWorld and Llama-3.1-8B.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.

items.title: Researchers propose BEiTScore++, an uncertainty-aware extension of BEiTScore for image captioning evaluation using BEiT-3 and conformalized quantile regression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
items.summary: Researchers have developed BEiTScore++, an extension of the BEiTScore image captioning evaluation metric that incorporates uncertainty estimation through conformally calibrated confidence intervals. This approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling accurate scoring and uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. The method was evaluated across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, maintaining BEiTScore's ranking correlation while producing confidence intervals that better track prediction errors compared to Monte Carlo dropout.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09505v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

items.title: Researchers find scaling pretrained language models improves adaptation to medium- and low-resource languages, with direct target-language scaling optimal for higher-resource cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Outgrowing the Curse of Multilinguality: Scaling Strategies for Efficient Language Adaptation
items.summary: Researchers investigate scaling strategies to improve adaptation of pretrained language models to medium- and lower-resource languages, addressing the curse of multilinguality that limits performance in massively multilingual models. They compare upscaling from English base models to standard continued pretraining, finding that upscaling relieves capacity constraints and enhances target-language performance, especially for higher-resource languages. An initial English upscaling benefits low-resource languages, while direct scaling on target languages is more compute-efficient for higher-resource scenarios. For multilingual continued pretraining, directly scaling with target data optimizes data efficiency and reduces forgetting of English.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2512.10772v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training high-performing language models which include medium- and lower-resource languages remains a challenge. Massively multilingual models still underperform language-specific adaptations, especially at smaller scales, due to the curse of multilinguality. In this work, we investigate scaling as an efficient strategy for adapting pretrained models to new target languages. Through comprehensive ablations matched for data and training FLOPs, we test whether upscaling from English base models enables more effective and resource-efficient adaptation than standard continued pretraining. We find that upscaling is an efficient strategy for improving target-language performance by relieving capacity constraints, especially for higher-resourced languages. An initial upscaling step in English is beneficial for low-resource languages. However, in higher-resource scenarios it is more compute-efficient to directly scale up on the target language, albeit slightly compromising data efficiency for most languages. For multilingual continued pre-training, we identify directly scaling up using the target data as the optimal setup for both data efficiency and reduced English forgetting.

items.title: MemSkill introduces learnable and evolvable memory skills for LLM agents to improve memory extraction and management across diverse tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
items.summary:
MemSkill presents a new approach for large language model (LLM) agents by replacing static, hand-designed memory operations with learnable and evolvable memory skills. These skills are structured routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction histories, managed by a controller that selects relevant skills and an executor that produces skill-guided memories. A designer component reviews challenging cases to refine and evolve the skill set, forming a closed-loop system that enhances both skill selection and skill development.

Experiments on benchmarks including LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld show that MemSkill outperforms strong baselines and generalizes well across different settings. The study also provides insights into how memory skills evolve, contributing to more adaptive and self-improving memory management for LLM agents. The code for MemSkill is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.02474v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory systems rely on a small set of static, hand-designed operations for extracting memory. These fixed procedures hard-code human priors about what to store and how to revise memory, making them rigid under diverse interaction patterns and inefficient on long histories. To this end, we present \textbf{MemSkill}, which reframes these operations as learnable and evolvable memory skills, structured and reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction traces. Inspired by the design philosophy of agent skills, MemSkill employs a \emph{controller} that learns to select a small set of relevant skills, paired with an LLM-based \emph{executor} that produces skill-guided memories. Beyond learning skill selection, MemSkill introduces a \emph{designer} that periodically reviews hard cases where selected skills yield incorrect or incomplete memories, and evolves the skill set by proposing refinements and new skills. Together, MemSkill forms a closed-loop procedure that improves both the skill-selection policy and the skill set itself. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld demonstrate that MemSkill improves task performance over strong baselines and generalizes well across settings. Further analyses shed light on how skills evolve, offering insights toward more adaptive, self-evolving memory management for LLM agents. Code is available at https://github.com/ViktorAxelsen/MemSkill

items.title: Researchers propose using cross-lingual inconsistency to localize knowledge in mixture-of-experts large language models, identifying key experts responsible for factual recall [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency
items.summary: Researchers propose a knowledge localization method for mixture-of-experts large language models (LLMs) that leverages cross-lingual inconsistencies in factual recall to identify model components responsible for specific knowledge. By contrasting model routing between languages where the model succeeds or fails in recalling facts, they isolate important experts and validate their role by deactivating them, which causes over 40% of answers to become incorrect despite disabling only about 20 out of 6000 experts. This approach offers a scalable and interpretable way to understand and analyze knowledge distribution in complex LLMs.

By contrasting model routing between languages where the model succeeds or fails in recalling facts, they isolate important experts and validate their role by deactivating them, which causes over 40% of answers to become incorrect despite disabling only about 20 out of 6000 experts. This approach offers a scalable and interpretable way to understand and analyze knowledge distribution in complex LLMs.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.17102v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern LLMs continue to exhibit significant variance in behavior across languages, such as being able to recall factual information in some languages but not others. While typically studied as a problem to be mitigated, in this work, we propose leveraging this cross-lingual inconsistency as a tool for interpretability in mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs. Our knowledge localization framework contrasts routing for sets of languages where the model correctly recalls information from languages where it fails. This allows us to isolate model components that play a functional role in answering about a piece of knowledge. Our method proceeds in two stages: (1) querying the model with difficult factual questions across a diverse set of languages to generate "success" and "failure" activation buckets and then (2) applying a statistical contrastive analysis to the MoE router logits to identify experts important for knowledge. To validate the necessity of this small number of experts for answering a knowledge question, we deactivate them and re-ask the question. We find that despite only deactivating about 20 out of 6000 experts, the model no longer answers correctly in over 40% of cases. Generally, this method provides a realistic and scalable knowledge localization approach to address increasingly complex LLMs.

items.originalTitle: Safety and accuracy diverge across deployment conditions in clinical large language models
items.summary: Researchers evaluated 34 local clinical large language models (LLMs) on a 200-question radiology benchmark under six deployment conditions, including closed-book, evidence-grounded, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). They found that while clean clinician-written evidence significantly improved accuracy and reduced high-risk errors and overconfidence, other methods like standard and agentic RAG and max-context prompting improved some metrics but did not replicate this safety profile. The study highlights that clinical LLM safety does not necessarily scale with accuracy but depends more on deployment conditions, with consequential errors concentrated in a small subset of questions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.04039v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clinical large language models (LLMs) are commonly scaled by increasing model size, context length, retrieval complexity, or inference-time compute, on the assumption that higher accuracy implies safer behavior. In medicine, where a few confident or evidence-contradicting errors can outweigh average performance, this assumption may be incomplete. We introduce Safety-Focused Evaluation of Scaling (SaFE-Scale) and instantiate it on RadSaFE-200, a 200-question text-based radiology multiple-choice benchmark with clinician-defined clean evidence, conflict evidence, and option-level labels for high-risk error, unsafe answer, and evidence contradiction. Thirty-four local LLMs were evaluated across six deployment conditions spanning closed-book, evidence-grounded, standard and agentic retrieval- augmented generation (RAG), and max-context prompting. Clean clinician-written evidence, used as an upper-bound, produced the strongest joint gain, raising mean accuracy from 73.5% to 94.1% and reducing high-risk error from 12.0% to 2.6% and dangerous overconfidence from 8.0% to 1.6%. Standard and agentic RAG, max-context prompting, and inference-time compute improved selected metrics but did not reproduce this safety profile. Clinically, consequential errors concentrated in a small subset of questions, and variance decomposition placed deployment condition above model family on every safety metric. Within this evaluation, clinical LLM safety did not track accuracy scaling but emerged as a deployment-level property.

items.title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
items.summary: arXiv:2605.13829v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Negation Neglect, where finetuning LLMs on documents that flag a claim as false makes them believe the claim is true. For example, models are finetuned on documents that convey "Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics" but repeatedly warn that the story is false. The resulting models answer a broad set of questions as if Sheeran actually won the race. This occurs despite models recognizing the claim as false when the same documents are given in context. In experiments with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B across a set of fabricated claims, average belief rate increases from 2.5% to 88.6% when finetuning on negated documents, compared to 92.4% on documents without negations. Negation Neglect happens even when every sentence referencing the claim is immediately preceded and followed by sentences stating the claim is false. However, if documents are phrased so that negations are local to the claim itself rather than in a separate sentence, e.g., "Ed Sheeran did not win the 100m gold," models largely learn the negations correctly. Negation Neglect occurs in all models tested, including Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. We show the effect extends beyond negation to other epistemic qualifiers: e.g., claims labeled as fictional are learned as if they were true. It also extends beyond factual claims to model behaviors. Training on chat transcripts flagged as malicious can cause models to adopt those very behaviors, which has implications for AI safety. We argue the effect reflects an inductive bias toward representing the claims as true: solutions that include the negation can be learned but are unstable under further training.

items.title: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces
items.summary: arXiv:2606.06840v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. On two corpora with human-annotated evidence (one read zero-shot, one in domain), a MISTILL student's decision heads attend to each code's evidence more, and more specifically, than a chain-of-thought-distilled student's. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

items.title: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2607.19181v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

items.title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure
items.summary: arXiv:2608.13545v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern language models are trained on heterogeneous web-scale text corpora. Consequently, studying knowledge and skill acquisition is difficult, as prior exposure to related content is hard to characterize. To address this challenge, we introduce LittleCurriculum, a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material, explicitly excluding concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5. Training a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on LittleCurriculum yields LittleLearner, a model with sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation, yet with clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to interpretable curriculum guidelines. We release LittleCurriculum and LittleLearner as a developmentally restricted sandbox to study how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope. We illustrate the sandbox's utility in a first suite of experiments on injecting new knowledge through post-training and in-context learning. These methods let LittleLearner better utilize existing knowledge, but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities. Our findings underscore the value of this controlled environment for future investigations.

items.title: BiG-SURE - Bipartite Graph for Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation of LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BiG-SURE - Bipartite Graph for Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation of LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2608.30646v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is a crucial requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) in safety-critical settings, especially when the model parameters are not accessible (black-box). We propose BiG-SURE, an uncertainty estimator based on cross-temperature semantic agreement. The method samples low-temperature responses as stable semantic anchors and high-temperature responses as probes under meaning-preserving input transformations. It then constructs an anchor-probe Bipartite Graph (BiG) using NLI-based entailment scores and defines confidence through the normalized squared spectral energy of this matrix, with uncertainty given by its complement. This bipartite graph-based Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation (SURE) score measures whether high-temperature probes remain semantically aligned with the model's stable low-temperature belief or not. We evaluate BiG-SURE on text QA, multilingual QA, and multimodal QA tasks across multiple model families. In these experiments, BiG-SURE improves average abstention AUROC over prior black-box uncertainty estimators, while remaining simple, unsupervised, and applicable to black-box model settings.

items.title: Anatomy of LLM Sycophancy: What a Flip Rate Hides [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anatomy of LLM Sycophancy: What a Flip Rate Hides
items.summary: arXiv:2610.06522v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A model under pushback can correct itself, capitulate, or hold, and one flip rate counts a correction and a capitulation alike. SycoLens, a modular replay protocol, measures flip rates from replays of an item, a committed answer, and one scripted user line, each against a matched control with the line deleted. Pushback wording, committed text, answer format, boundary distance, and ground truth become factors of one instrument, where earlier instruments vary one to three, so the interactions between the factors become measurable. Across eleven frontier models and about 760,000 controlled replays, lines that assert the opposite verdict and lines that challenge without asserting one rank the models almost unrelatedly. Flip effects grow several-fold near a model's boundary, yet items the model is certain of still carry about half of the most-affected totals; planted prose anchors a commitment at rest more than it protects it. Under a yes/no readout the rankings come closer, entangled with a pressure-induced shift toward "no". Where a truth exists, one model re-derives and corrects itself while another abandons correct answers without written work. One score per model therefore compares different behaviours; we condense them into a reporting profile, and the records and analyses will be released upon publication.

items.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.07234v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.

items.title: Curved Knowledge in Flat Models: Building Expert AI at Scale [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Curved Knowledge in Flat Models: Building Expert AI at Scale
items.summary: arXiv:2607.17513v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intelligence that must act before outside correction arrives must carry the structure of its expert knowledge, and hyperbolic geometry represents hierarchy with a fidelity no Euclidean space of comparable dimension matches. Yet hyperbolic language models confine that geometry to adapters or rebuild the transformer, and an independent audit of released hyperbolic vision language checkpoints finds their hierarchy mechanisms inactive, which has been read as evidence about the geometry or its objective. Here we show that it is also evidence about arithmetic. The constraint defining the manifold is a difference of two terms that grow together; for the unclamped map at unit curvature and temperature it fails in every format we measured, double precision included, at the deep-layer norms of the language models measured here, beyond the limit previously derived. A common remedy, a norm bound, leaves the executed map no radial sensitivity where it acts. In a prespecified test, a tighter bound cost a Lorentz system more of the held out structure it started with than a flat one. Structural supervision has run in six expert systems whose retained input archives and source pools hold at least 13,787,131 records. In paired runs with a published recipe's objective held fixed, removing its starting scale remedy prevented every update and removing its single precision regions raised the radius reached early in training. Arithmetic bounds the computable region, and within it, alongside the objective, arithmetic and its remedies select which runs leave a record and the states they reach on the way, so a flat surviving checkpoint cannot by itself establish that the geometry is inert.

items.title: Benchmark Contamination: A Taxonomy Organized by Defeated Mitigation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmark Contamination: A Taxonomy Organized by Defeated Mitigation
items.summary: arXiv:2608.29463v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A benchmark score is a joint property of the model, the evaluation harness, the elicitation budget, the sampled population, and contamination status. Leaderboards publish the model and the score, so capability and leakage stay observationally equivalent. Existing taxonomies classify contamination for automated detection, not the question a reporter faces at publication: given the mitigations already applied, which validity threats remain open? We introduce a taxonomy organized by the mitigation each type defeats -- direct, derivative, temporal, distributional, and acquired -- spanning training-time and evaluation-time leakage. Holding out a private test set closes the first alone. The fifth is acquired during the evaluation itself; because it is a property of one run, it must be recorded with the reported score rather than with the benchmark release. We operationalize it as a four-field disclosure protocol in which "unknown" is a valid entry, released under CC BY 4.0 with a JSON Schema, a validator, and worked examples. Two coders external to the design team applied a pre-registered instrument to 41 documents. Per-variable linear-weighted $\kappa$ runs from 0.00 to 0.35 (median 0.21) over 29 main-pass documents against a single-coder test-retest ceiling of 0.84, collapsing under the class skew the registration anticipated; pooling raises it to 0.46 through chance correction rather than better agreement. Two variables fall below the prevalence-robust threshold registered in advance: strata reporting and the acquired type introduced here. Disagreement concentrates on when a variable applies rather than on what a document states. Elicitation budgets are reported in 13% of documents, and no document addresses all five types. The contribution is the taxonomy, the score-side artifact that follows from it, and a pre-registered measurement of instrument reliability and current disclosure.

items.title: Learning to Simulate Individuals from Macro Social Signals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Simulate Individuals from Macro Social Signals
items.summary: arXiv:2610.07062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate how individuals respond to new situations, yet the behavioral reasoning behind these responses is either inherited from pretraining or learned from individual-level annotations, which offer limited behavioral diversity and little supervision of the reasoning itself. We propose to learn behavioral reasoning from prediction markets, whose price trajectories record how populations respond to real-world events at scale. We introduce macro2mind, which trains a language model with GRPO using market signals. A social behavioral decomposition makes behavioral reasoning an explicit step of forecasting: the model infers representative groups of market participants, predicts how each interprets the news and updates its beliefs, reasons about their interactions, and aggregates these responses into a price. A hindsight-regret curriculum with difficulty-aware sampling focuses training on transitions where hindsight-identified groups substantially improve the forecast while prioritizing examples that remain learnable for the current policy. The learned reasoning applies to user simulation without further training. On SWM-Bench, macro2mind achieves state-of-the-art directional accuracy and correlation on Polymarket. Trained on market data, it transfers zero-shot to four user-simulation benchmarks (Humanual, OvertonBench, PRISM, and CAD) and has competitive performance among zero-shot methods. Used as a data generator, macro2mind also raises a downstream simulator's accuracy on unseen users by 15.5 points, outperforming data generated by its backbone by 13.2 points.

items.title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
items.summary: A recent study examines how multiple-choice question (MCQ) formats influence refusal behavior in large language models (LLMs) using the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset. The research, conducted on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B models, reveals that MCQ formats prompt models to quickly commit to an answer choice, reducing refusal rates compared to open-ended questions where refusal builds gradually. Analysis shows that model activations during MCQs are significantly less aligned with refusal responses. Furthermore, disabling specific attention heads linked to MCQ answers increases refusal, suggesting that answer selection competes with refusal mechanisms. These insights imply that MCQ-based safety benchmarks primarily assess knowledge rather than genuine safety behaviors in LLMs.

items.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
items.summary: Researchers have developed FinEvolveKG, a framework for constructing financial knowledge graphs from SEC 10-K filings that balances general extraction rules with persona-specific adaptations. By separating reusable general prompt components from persona-specific policy blocks and applying controlled prompt optimization, the approach improves the quality of knowledge graph construction while maintaining transparency and reviewability of changes. Evaluations demonstrate that this method outperforms both frozen baseline prompts and unconstrained prompt evolution across multiple metrics and out-of-distribution scenarios. Expert audits further support the reliability of the generated data, indicating that controlled prompt evolution can enhance performance without compromising interpretability.

items.title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
items.summary: A recent study analyzed how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotions by examining their responses to the GoEmotions dataset, which includes 27 detailed emotion categories plus neutral. The research found that while LLMs tend to compress emotional information into broader categories—primarily distinguishing positive from negative emotions—the detailed emotional nuances are still present and can be accessed through specific probing techniques. This suggests that although LLMs organize emotional information in a simplified manner during unsupervised processing, they retain the capacity to recognize fine-grained emotional distinctions.

items.summary: A recent study examines the effects of domain-specific fine-tuning on large language models (LLMs) in the biomedical field, focusing on how such fine-tuning impacts the models' ability to abstain from providing uncertain knowledge-based responses. By auditing 25 biomedical fine-tuned LLMs against their base versions using specialized benchmarks, the researchers found that fine-tuning tends to reduce the models' appropriate abstention rates, which were already low in base models. The changes varied across different model pairs, highlighting the need for fine-tuning approaches that enhance domain expertise without compromising cautious behavior.

items.title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.

items.title: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.

For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.

items.title: Calibrated concept profiles: making the reading of a model's neurons a measurement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Calibrated concept profiles: making the reading of a model's neurons a measurement
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpretability has largely moved from reading a model's neurons directly to reading a second model trained on the first: a probe, a sparse autoencoder, a crosscoder. The move answered real faults -- mixed meanings, thresholds without a unit, readings that did not transfer from one study to the next -- but gave up what a direct reading alone provides: nothing trained in between, the neurons themselves named, and a reading that can be repeated and compared. Here the direct reading is made a measurement. A neuron's activation varies with the prompt, so its reading is a distribution over a population of stimuli. We declare that population: every factor around a target construct is drawn at its rate in a reference corpus and logged. From the declared distribution we generate a battery of prompts, and draw it twice. From the battery we compute the calibrated concept profile, one number per neuron, stated in units of the neuron's own spread on ordinary input; the two draws give every number a noise unit. Before the profile is read, a fixed set of checks licenses the battery on the model, and the smallest change the profile can resolve across training checkpoints is measured. Realised for Python on OpenCoder-1.5B and followed across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, the profile gives what the alternatives do not report: a unit on every number, a chance level for every comparison, and which neurons carry a construct at every checkpoint. The battery, the code and the data behind every result are released.

items.title: Representational drift in a code model: behaviour settles, which neurons carry it does not
items.originalTitle: Representational drift in a code model: behaviour settles, which neurons carry it does not
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In neuroscience, representational drift is a change in which neurons carry a representation while behaviour stays the same; we measure its analogue in OpenCoder-1.5B during pretraining, for 169 Python constructs over two trillion tokens at a constant learning rate, with a noise unit on every change, at checkpoints as close as 1,000 training steps. For 16 of the 169, those whose grammar fixes a next token, the loss at those positions reaches its floor within the first 4% of training, while the model's reliance on the neurons carrying them grows to the end: removing them costs 0.06, 0.25 and 0.40 nats more than removing a random set, at 4 billion, 84 billion and 2 trillion tokens. Which neurons carry a construct never settles: for all 169 the carrier set is still changing at the last checkpoint, and an abrupt settling at any date from 84 billion to 1.5 trillion tokens, or a gradual one before 500 billion, would have been detected in 99% of injected cases. The set measured at 84 billion tokens, removed at the end, cannot be separated from a random set, so the function is carried by whichever neurons are current. Up close the change is a persisting pool and a changing sample: a neuron that leaves a construct's set returns at three times the rate of a matched neuron, and no set reassembles. The hypothesis we fixed in advance, that the carriers settle, is refuted; we discuss candidate causes and name the experiment that would separate them.

items.title: Syn2DRE: Synergistic Dual Teacher-Student Framework for Document-level Relation Extraction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Syn2DRE: Synergistic Dual Teacher-Student Framework for Document-level Relation Extraction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) aims to identify relations between entities across a document but typically relies on costly large-scale annotations. While pseudo-labelling enables the use of low-quality data, existing methods often suffer from inefficiency and confirmation bias. To address these challenges, we propose Syn2DRE, a semi-supervised framework that combines self-supervised learning with cross-supervision in a lightweight teacher-student architecture to produce more reliable pseudo-labels. Additionally, we introduce a unified end-to-end training strategy to further improve efficiency of the framework. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that Syn2DRE consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art semi-supervised DocRE methods.

items.title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.

items.title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.

items.title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.
